_comment: Internal test-quality tool — NOT part of the published package and not
something adopters ever see (no docs page, no handbook section, no emitted
config). It answers one question about THIS repo's own suite: 100% line
coverage says every line ran, not that a wrong line would be caught.
StringLiteral is excluded, and the reason is a measured line rather than a
blanket claim. Enabling it repo-wide gives 87.79% against 97.86% (6808
mutants against 4574): 2234 of them are string literals, and 731 of those
survive. Those 731 are two different things:
1. A discrete contract per literal. Every member of an allowlist is one:
`NON_SOURCE_DIRS` losing `dist/` makes inspect scan the build output;
`ESLINT_FILES` losing `eslint.config.ts` makes detect miss a config that
exists; `REACTIVE_API` losing `toRefs` makes a composable using it report
as a pure function. Same for the remedy half of a rule message, and for
the `note` that labels each planned action. These ARE tested — as ordinary
assertions, so they hold whether or not this mutator runs.
2. Prose. `cli`'s USAGE and seven *_HELP bodies are 214 of the survivors on
their own; presets' layer descriptions are another 78; the rest are middle
sentences of long instructs. Pinning those literally would make the tests
a copy of the text — snapshot testing through the back door, in a suite
that deliberately has none. What matters about prose is whether an agent
reads it and does the right thing, and that is what `src/conformance`
(known scenarios) and `npm run field:run` (new ones) exist to answer.
So the exclusion is a boundary between two kinds of check, not a gap: group
1 is covered by tests that do not depend on this setting, and group 2 is not
a unit-test question. Re-measure with `mutator.excludedMutations: []` if that
reasoning needs re-testing; the numbers above are from the commit that wrote
this comment.
